item.title: 7 Real Portland Locations From 'Wildwood'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The creators behind the stop-motion film Wildwood took 16 years to painstakingly craft every detail of the transportive fantasy epic. Based on a book by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis, Wildwood tells the tale of a young girl named Prue whose brother is plucked from the ground by crows. Undeterred, she and her initially hapless sidekick Curtis venture into the wilderness to find him.

What follows is a surreal journey through a land where animals talk, trees are worshiped, coyotes wield cannons, and the dead returnâalbeit not always to their original forms. Interspersed throughout are recognizable landmarks from the city of Portland, Oregon, which add a sense of modernity and charm to the book and film.

I visited Portland to trace the real-world locations that found their way into Wildwood. Here are some of them.

Forest Park

Meloy and Ellis conceptualized the story on their many walks through Portlandâs Forest Park. From the first moment I spotted the wall of infinite shades of green rising up almost directly from the city streets, I could see why this place lent itself to imaginal flights of fancy.

It was a crisp autumn morning, a sheen of rain still on the ground. I had started my morning with a latte and breakfast burrito at the quaint Haven Coffee Co., so I was feeling pleasantly energized as I walked down a street lined with orange trees.Â

My guide from Around Portland Tours seemed to know everything about the area. We passed a hill overlooking a cluster of factories that provided the inspiration for the Industrial Wastes in Wildwood. They had been built on a former wetland, my guide informed me. In the book, these are a mysterious cluster of factories and warehouses that act as a barrier between Portland and the so-called Impassable Wilderness beyond.Â

Barely a minute later, we were inside another realmâa kingdom of trees. Towering Douglas firs and cedars soared towards the sky. Dewy ferns and huckleberry bushes shimmered, massive orange maple leaves coated the ground, and countless types of mushrooms covered fallen trees in the process of decomposing and becoming new life.Â

I have always felt uniquely at peace in forests, and this one was no exception; a sense of deep calm and presence washed over me immediately. Forest bathingâor the practice of wandering through a forest, exploring it with all your sensesâis an increasingly popular way to reduce stress and improve health, my guide explained, and this one felt like the perfect place to do just that.Â

The fact that the forest stood so close to bustling city streets made it feel all the more otherworldly, as if we truly had stepped through a portal from the human world into something much wilder and older.

The woods of the Pacific Northwest have long inspired various tales of cryptids such as Sasquatch, and I didnât have to look far to see withered, gnarled trunks or mossy stones that resembled various mythical creatures. This was the forestâs domain, and even human-made structures were all in the process of being reclaimed. We paused for a while at the dilapidated Witchâs Cabin, a former outpost rapidly being swallowed by moss and lichens. Altars made of stones, books, and Polaroids filled the crumbling windows.

Then we continued deeper and higher up into the woods. At one point, I caught a tiny glimpse of a house poking through the tall trees. That was the house originally used as the Cullensâ home in the first Twilight movie, my guide informed me, and indeed it wasn't too hard to imagine vampires leaping through these trees.

We continued our climb. The beauty was near-indescribable; the forest consisted of countless colors that shone far brighter in real life than in any of my photos. The air filling my lungs was clean, alive. I wanted to stay, to continue to wander through all 5,200 acres of the United Statesâ largest urban park.

The Bird Alliance

Our first stop within Forest Park was the Bird Alliance, which served as the inspiration for Wildwood's Avian Principality, or the kingdom of birds. Formerly the Audubon Society, this 150-acre expanse of land is dedicated to protecting birds and connecting people to nature.

We made our way down to a large enclosure, which I knew was home to the bird that inspired the noble Owl Rex in Wildwood. At first we couldnât spot her. The enclosure was large, filled with various perches, fauna, and equipment, and had wire mesh walls that looked out onto the forest.Â

Suddenly I realized that she had been perched on a branch directly above us the whole time, almost as if she had specifically been waiting for our appointment. Julio was a Great Horned Owl who looked remarkably regal, with round golden eyes that burned with intelligence. The plaque beside her explained she had been rescued as a young owl and never learned how to successfully be wild, which was why she spent her days here.Â

Her head swiveled backward, and she stretched out her scalloped wings for a moment. It was not hard at all to see why Meloy and Ellis had thought to model the Crown Prince of the Avian Principality after her. As we left, I felt somehow obligated to thank her for her presence. I then bought a bird-themed puzzle at a quaint gift shop, and then we ventured back into the woods.

Pittock Mansion

We then made our way up Wildwood Trail, the path that inspired the name of Meloy and Ellisâs book. The forest seemed to grow deeper and ever-wilder, until a mansion emerged out of nowhere.

It was grand, built in the French Renaissance style with smooth sandstone walls, and I recognized it immediately. I had seen the film Wildwood just two days before, and now I had the strange feeling that Iâd stepped directly into a scene from it. The experience was disorienting, as if the lines between reality and story had blurred ever-so slightly.

Pittock Mansion was built in 1914 for Oregonian publisher and businessman Henry Pittock and his wife Georgiana, a philanthropist who founded the Portland Rose Society. The mansion is rumored to be haunted by both Henry and Georgianaâs spirits, among others, and today it is preserved as a museum and event space.

We sat by the edge of the grounds, looking down over Portland and towards the towering Mount Hood, which was veiled in clouds. The mountain hasnât been as snowy as usual in recent years, my guide said, and we both were quiet for a while. I thought of the droughts and wildfires that had filled the news recently. Wildwood, I reflected, is not only about fanciful forest adventures; itâs also about human greed and violence, and the dangers of taking what does not belong to you. âWhen you mess with nature,â my guide said, using more colorful language in reality to effectively sum up one of Wildwoodâs core messages, âit messes back.â

I had thought we might walk back through the woods, but instead we made our way down a winding street that led us past a series of impressively elegant mansions, all staring out over the city. Then, all at once, we arrived at a bus station beside a bustling highway. Minutes later, we were back among the skyscrapers and gas stations of the metropolitan world.

I felt like Iâd just been somewhere secret and magical yet profoundly real and alive, and this world of humans and cars felt more like the dream. I had been entertaining the idea of leaving the city to live closer to nature for some time, and this experience, among other things, made me sure that my next home would be somewhere closer to the woods.

St. Johns Bridge

That afternoon, I made my way over towards St. Johns, the neighborhood where Meloy and Ellis lived while writing Wildwood. Rain clouds were gathering, but I had my umbrella and decided to brave it. It was drizzling when I got out near the bridge.Â…

item.title: The Most Common European Ancestry in Every State, Mapped
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country. But some states had one country's ancestors dominate over the others when it comes to where residents can trace their roots.

The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.

Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.

Germany

German immigrants have been coming to the United States since before the United States existed. A group of Quaker families arrived in 1683 and founded Germantown, which is now a suburb of Philadelphia. The largest wave, however, came in the 1800s when Germans arrived with hopes of securing land to farm or leave after a failed revolution in 1848. They brought with them things like kindergarten, the tradition of Christmas trees, and hot dogs.

Today, an estimated 40 to 60 million Americans consider German their main heritage, making it the largest country of origin for immigration. It's even more than Irish or Italian heritage and is the main European heritage in 27 states, more than any other European group. German roots are mainly found in the Midwest and West Coast.

England

Another strong country for where Americans claim roots is England. After all, England provided some of the earliest settlers across the Atlantic along the East Coast, with colonists first arriving in Jamestown in modern-day Virginia in 1607.

English roots dominate the South, with states in the Southeast claiming English heritage over all other European countries. English pockets also remain in New England, like Maine and Vermont, as well as out west in New Mexico, Utah, and Idaho.

Ireland

Irish immigration peaked in the United States in the mid-1800s, when the Great Famine ravaged the country. It's estimated that between 1851 and 1860, more than 80% of immigrants arriving in the United States came from Ireland. Additional near-famines in the second half of the 1800s propped up the flow of immigrants from Ireland to the United States.

Those migration waves left a lasting effect on the East Coast, where five states still claim Irish heritage as the most common European heritage. States where Ireland is the most represented European heritage include Delaware, the District of Columbia, and the New England states of New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. Even New York, which is known for its diverse population in New York City, cites Ireland as the country that produced the highest number of ancestral European roots among residents.

Italy

Only two states claim Italy as the most common European ancestor among their residents, with East Coast states Connecticut and New Jersey representing the country.

Italians arrived in the United States most notably in the 20th century. But while other immigrants came through New York City and moved inland, Italian immigrants stayed in the area, with an estimated one-third settling around New York City.

In New Jersey, almost 1.3 million residents claim some sort of Italian ancestry, pushing it past Irish ancestry by more than 100,000 residents.

Connecticut has a similar dynamic, with Italian heritage outnumbering Irish ancestry, and both groups clearly leading the state.

France

Louisiana is the only state that claims French ancestry more than any other European ancestry among residents.

France had already established itself in Louisiana before the 1800s, but the Louisiana Purchase solidified Louisiana's placeâand its French traditionsâin American life. The 1803 purchase included parts of several states as far as modern-day Montana and Minnesota, but Louisiana in particular held on to its French roots after the handover of land.

item.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people.

The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains.

I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story.

A growing trend

One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes.

My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults.

The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion.

Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down

Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price.

Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people.

That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.”

Family caregivers pay a price

Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460.

But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones.

Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits.

Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one.

AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities.

A ‘daughterhood penalty’

Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax.

Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability.

Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives.

But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing.

Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-20 19:58 UTC

item.title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men.

That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by David Walliams, accusations Walliams denies. There was earnest discussion of the enabling power of celebrity, how stardust blinds people from seeing what’s in front of them. Some suggested the problem was narrower still, with abuse cast as a function of the way British comedy operates, lacking a recognisable HR structure or protection for junior workers from big names with clout. In parallel, a debate began about staggering the age of consent, addressing the particular dynamics of older men who target younger women, including those who would be regarded as children by any definition except the letter of the law.

All of those are valid questions, by the way. But if, underlying them, is the consoling hope that we are facing a limited problem, one confined to, say, high-status men or those whose victims are very young, then Thursday’s verdicts should dispel it. The grimmer truth is that this problem is wider and deeper: the guilty were ordinary men, carpenters and cabbies, ready to violate a middle-aged woman who was audibly and visibly unconscious.

Even this especially shocking crime – in which a man recruits other men online to rape his sedated wife – may not be as rare as we imagine. A similar case is now being tried in Manchester and, according to Wiltshire police: “This may be a significantly under-reported crime type.”

Of course, there are specific elements and contexts that make rape and sexual abuse more possible. Just as the entertainment industry provided a hospitable environment for Brand, so Philip Young could advertise for fellow rapists thanks to online forums such as Craigslist and Reddit. The internet made it easier for him to secure sedative drugs. But these things facilitate rather than drive the impulse. They are not the heart of the matter. Which is, to state it plainly, male hatred of women.

Of course, such hatred is not universal; not every man is infected by it. But it is embedded in our world and sits deep in our culture. (After Pelicot and Young, you look again at Sleeping Beauty: what exactly did we think was going on in a story that, in its 17th-century telling, had the king discover the unmoving, unconscious body of a woman, rape and impregnate that woman, and then flee?)

In Afghanistan, the Taliban have imposed gender apartheid, prohibiting girls and women from learning, singing, taking a bus without a man or walking to the park. According to Human Rights Watch, one directive ordered the removal of windows, lest Afghan women, “imprisoned in their homes, might see the outside world”. Closer to hand, you look at the manosphere, whose leading lights delight in the degradation and humiliation of women, treating their girlfriends as, at best, unpaid domestic servants or, at worst, property and chattel. You contemplate the rates of femicide, which include three women killed every fortnight in England and Wales by a current or former partner. You look at the rape statistics, including the estimate from the Centre for Women’s Justice (CWJ) that only 15% of all rapes get reported and that, of those that do, only a tiny percentage ultimately ends in a conviction.

Women have been saying all this, loudly and clearly, for years. When cases such as Brand or Walliams or Philip Young erupt, it tends to be women who lead the debate and make the arguments, in print and on the airwaves. On one level, that’s obvious – in the same way that, say, Jewish voices are given the floor when there is a murderous attack on Jews. But it’s also incomplete. Because it misses out, and risks letting off the hook, those who have most work to do. In this case, men.

The logic of that was encapsulated well by a small sign – no more than an A4 piece of paper – held up by a woman protesting in New York earlier this year over the case of the Cornell seven: the fraternity brothers at Cornell University accused of gang-raping a female student they’d incapacitated through ketamine, and doing so over the course of seven hours. The protester’s sign carried three words that had been crossed out: Protect Your Daughters. In their place were three different words: Educate Your Sons.

This shifts responsibility to where it should lie. It honours the principle articulated so concisely by Gisèle Pelicot herself who, like Joanne Young, waived her right to anonymity, believing there was no need to hide herself since she had nothing to be ashamed of. Or, as she put it, “Shame has to change sides.”

That makes moral sense, but it might make practical sense too. Take the kind of young man susceptible to the example of Andrew Tate and his fellow denizens of the manosphere. If such a man hears a woman condemn misogyny, if they hear a woman speak of the necessity of consent, they will hear those as messages that stand in opposition to manliness. They will understand their own sexual desires as manly and restraints on those desires as their opposite, as unmanly or feminine. For a man such as this, it is perhaps only condemnation by other men, framed in terms of maleness, that will cut through.

A useful precedent could be what was, in a different era, called wife-beating. Not so long ago, the culture all but countenanced such behaviour. Think of the Beatles’ song, Run For Your Life, both its title and lyric: “Well, I’d rather see you dead, little girl / Than to be with another man”. But attitudes moved. “The norm did shift,” CWJ founder Harriet Wistrich told me on Friday. These days, if a man were hitting his partner in sight of another man, that second man would, she hopes, step in.

This, then, is how fathers might best heed that protester’s call to educate their sons. To tell them that the kind of behaviour that has been revealed in courtrooms and on front pages these last two weeks is wicked and inhuman, but also pathetic, inadequate and weak – and, yes, worthy of shame. That to prey on those who have less power, or no power at all, is the mark of someone who is not merely a failure as a person – but no man at all.

- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

- Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

item.title: Did men evolve to fight each other? Scientists can’t agree.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Anthropologist David Puts was a graduate student trying to decide on a dissertation topic when inspiration struck him at a mall food court. While eating a cheeseburger, he overheard two men behind him speaking in unusually deep voices. “I turned around to see what was happening, and there was a young, good-looking female nearby,” Puts said.

His initial thought was that human males evolved deep voices to attract women, but he soon began to wonder whether they might also help establish dominance over other men: “A deep voice is intimidating — think about Darth Vader.” So, for his dissertation, Puts tested both possibilities. What he found surprised him.

Women tended to prefer a deeper, more masculine voice, but the effect of voice pitch on their ratings of male attractiveness wasn’t very big. Meanwhile, the effect of voice pitch on men’s judgment of another man’s dominance and fighting ability was 15 times bigger.

The unexpected result led Puts to revisit earlier studies. He noticed that “the literature was really biased towards female mate choice” as a reason for deep voices, while findings related to male-male competition seemed to get “pushed under the rug.” This realization became the foundation for Puts’ theory that competition between males for mates, also known as “male-male contest competition,” may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized.

Puts, now a professor of anthropology and psychology at Pennsylvania State University, has continued to think about and develop this theory ever since the seed for it was planted in his brain in that mall food court in the early 2000s. Although he said he is mostly driven by a fascination with human nature, there’s more to his theory than pure academic interest. He believes that evolutionary understanding might help explain aspects of male psychology and inform positive social change.

Competition between males for mates may have played a larger role in the evolution of the human male than scientists had previously recognized.

In November 2026, Puts and graduate student Saeed Koohgard published a review titled “The deadliest primate: Contest competition and the evolution of human males” in the Journal of Human Evolution. The review links modern-day male characteristics, including physical aggression, to male-male contest competition among our ancestors — a controversial theory.

Grateful for curious minds

This Thanksgiving, get 15% off Big Think membership and join a community of idea explorers. Use code BIGTHANKS15 at checkout. Valid on annual plans for new members only.

“This [idea] is supported primarily by evolutionary psychologists,” said Agustín Fuentes, an anthropologist at Princeton University. “Most anthropologists do not support this at all.” He said that those interested in understanding male violence should read the paper “but recognize this is a very teeny slice and a very biased view” in the midst of the wider anthropological, psychological, and sociological literature.

The ancestral mating system

For at least the past 150,000 years, the effective number of reproducing women at any given time has been roughly three times that of men, according to a 2015 study looking at Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA. This may reflect male invaders displacing local men, but Puts and Koohgard think it points to a polygynous mating system, where some men fathered children with several partners, while many other men had no children at all. They believe that our ancestors lived in single-male family units embedded within larger bands, as hamadryas and gelada baboons do.

This setup meant that “our male ancestors intensely fought, threatened, and killed each other to monopolize mates,” Puts said.

In their review, Puts and Koohgard cite several findings that are consistent with their theory. For example, in a study of Eurasian Neanderthal and early modern human remains from 80,000 to 20,000 years ago, men were about six times more likely than women to show signs of head injuries. Furthermore, a study of homicide data spanning two decades and four locations (Canada, England/Wales, Chicago, and Detroit) found that unrelated men kill each other 27 times more often than unrelated women kill each other.

“A lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

David Puts

Puts and Koohgard also point to several features of the male anatomy as complementary evidence of male-male contest competition. Men are larger than women on average, with 61% more muscle mass overall and 75% more upper-body muscle mass. Size and muscularity are traits that help win fights. Men also have what biologists call “badges of status,” such as facial hair and deep voices. These traits signal dominance and help to win resources, such as mates, without engaging in costly fights.

Puts and Koohgard argue that, together, these lines of evidence suggest that male-male contest competition has played an important role in shaping men’s behaviors, including physical aggression. People might hear this theory and misread it as a justification of male violence, Puts said, but he stresses that understanding evolutionary influences is not the same as condoning violence — the idea that something being natural or evolved makes it justified is what’s known as the “naturalistic fallacy.”

Although Puts and Koohgard’s theory centers on the idea that aggression helped our male ancestors to win mates, Puts doubts that the most violent males were ever the most successful. “There are huge costs to violence,” he said, “and if you’re living in a group and you’re a belligerent loose cannon, you’re likely to be killed or at least ostracized.” Instead, Puts thinks that “a lot of male mating success may have had to do with just the plausible threat of aggression.”

Clashing views

Fuentes is not convinced by Puts and Koohgard’s theory. The claim of a polygynous ancestral mating system is “highly disputed,” he said, and the “vast majority of geneticists who work in this area” conclude that our ancestors were most likely monogamous, with some mild polygyny.

He accused Puts and Koohgard of selectively citing works that support their theory while leaving out research that complicates or challenges it — their paper doesn’t mention Nam Kim and Marc Kissel’s book Emergent Warfare in Our Evolutionary Past, for example. That book frames violence as complex and dependent on multiple conditions — not simply an evolved male strategy. Citing it would make it “more complicated to make the argument that [they’re] making,” Fuentes said.

However, Raymond Hames, an emeritus professor of anthropology at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, praised Puts and Koohgard’s review as “very comprehensive.” He said the paper’s strength is that it tests several alternative hypotheses that might explain male traits, such as sexual division of labor, and finds them a poor fit. His only objection is to the paper’s title: “The deadliest primate.” “Although we are violent, we are not the deadliest of all primates,” Hames said. Red-tailed monkeys, blue monkeys, and red-fronted lemurs are all far more likely than humans to kill their own kind, according to a 2016 study.
